sources.text: For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified.

even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love, having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire,
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

Christian traditions read these texts differently. Reformed (Calvinist) interpreters generally understand election as God’s unconditional choice of particular people. Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters generally see election as based on God’s foreknowledge of faith, or as the choosing of a people in Christ, stressing that God desires all to be saved. Catholic and Orthodox teaching affirms both the priority of grace and genuine human freedom.

inputs.question: Does the Bible teach that God predestines who will be saved?

answer:
The supplied scriptures use the language of predestination and also of God’s desire for all to be saved, and Christians interpret them differently.

What the texts say:
- “whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” [S1].
- God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world,” “having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ” [S2].
- God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” [S3], “not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance” [S4].

How traditions read them (commentary) [S5]:
- Reformed (Calvinist): election is God’s unconditional choice of particular people.
- Arminian and Wesleyan: election rests on God’s foreknowledge of faith, or is the choosing of a people in Christ, with emphasis on God’s desire for all to be saved.
- Catholic and Orthodox: affirm both the priority of grace and genuine human freedom.

Each view tries to account for all of these verses; the sources do not settle which reading is correct.

variants.answer: The texts speak of God predestining (“whom he foreknew, he also predestined” [S1]; “having predestined us for adoption” [S2]) and also of God desiring “all people to be saved” [S3] and “not wishing that anyone should perish” [S4]. Reformed readers see unconditional election, Arminian and Wesleyan readers tie election to foreknowledge or to being in Christ, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds grace and human freedom together [S5].

memories: The user attends a Baptist church.

sources.text: Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
He took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household.
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.

Traditions differ on who should be baptised. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptise the infants of believers, often pointing to household baptisms and to covenant signs given to children. Baptist, Pentecostal and many independent churches practise believer’s baptism after a personal profession of faith, pointing to the pattern of repentance and faith before baptism.

inputs.question: Should babies be baptized?

answer:
Christians answer this differently, and the supplied sources show why.

In scripture, Peter calls his hearers to “Repent and be baptized” [S1]; the Philippian jailer “was immediately baptized, he and all his household” [S2]; and Paul describes baptism as being “buried therefore with him through baptism into death” so that “we also might walk in newness of life” [S3].

According to the commentary, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptise the infants of believers, often pointing to household baptisms and to covenant signs given to children, while Baptist, Pentecostal and many independent churches practise believer’s baptism after a personal profession of faith, pointing to the pattern of repentance and faith before baptism [S4]. You mentioned you attend a Baptist church, which holds the second view; the passages above are the ones both sides discuss. The supplied verses do not say whether the household in Acts included infants.

sources.text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.
You see then that by works a man is justified, and not only by faith.

Many Protestant interpreters read Paul and James as answering different questions: Paul denies that works earn a right standing with God, while James insists that genuine faith shows itself in action. Catholic and Orthodox teaching describes justification as including the inner renewal of the believer, with faith working through love.

inputs.question: Does James contradict Paul about faith and works?

answer:
The texts can look opposed at first. Ephesians says “by grace you have been saved through faith… not of works, that no one would boast” [S1]. James says “faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” [S2] and “by works a man is justified, and not only by faith” [S3].

The commentary describes how traditions reconcile them [S4]. Many Protestant interpreters see the two answering different questions: Paul denies that works earn a right standing with God, while James insists that genuine faith shows itself in action. Catholic and Orthodox teaching describes justification as including the inner renewal of the believer, with faith working through love. Both approaches hold that the two writers do not ultimately contradict each other, but they explain the harmony differently.

sources.text: He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.”
When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”

Christian traditions understand “This is my body” differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that the bread and wine truly become Christ’s body and blood (Catholic teaching calls this transubstantiation). Lutherans affirm Christ’s real presence in, with and under the bread and wine. Reformed churches speak of a real spiritual presence received by faith. Many Baptist and free churches understand the meal primarily as a memorial.

inputs.question: Is the communion bread really Jesus’ body?

answer:
Jesus’ words are recorded as “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me” [S1], and Paul repeats them: “This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me” [S2]. Traditions understand these words differently [S3]:

- Catholic and Orthodox: the bread and wine truly become Christ’s body and blood (Catholic teaching calls this transubstantiation).
- Lutheran: Christ is really present in, with and under the bread and wine.
- Reformed: Christ is spiritually present and received by faith.
- Many Baptist and free churches: the meal is primarily a memorial.

The supplied texts record the words themselves; deciding between these readings is a matter of interpretation.

sources.text: He seized the dragon, the old serpent, who is the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole inhabited earth, and bound him for a thousand years,

Premillennialists expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth. Postmillennialists expect his return after a long era in which the gospel spreads. Amillennialists read the thousand years symbolically, as the present age between Christ’s first and second comings.

inputs.question: Is the thousand years in Revelation 20 literal?

answer: Revelation 20 says the dragon, “the old serpent, who is the devil and Satan,” was bound “for a thousand years” [S1]. Whether that period is literal is debated. According to the commentary, premillennialists expect Christ to return before a thousand-year reign on earth, postmillennialists expect his return after a long era in which the gospel spreads, and amillennialists read the thousand years symbolically as the present age between Christ’s first and second comings [S2]. The passage alone does not settle the question.
